topic: Diffraction: why f/22 is softer than f/8 (Airy disk 2.44 x wavelength x f-number vs Canon R8 6 micron pixels; simulated Siemens star)
lines: Close your aperture more, and your photo gets softer.
A
Yes, really.
A
Light is a wave. Squeeze it through a tiny hole, and it spreads out.
B
One point of light becomes a fuzzy disc, with rings around it. It's called the Airy disk.
C
Its width is two point four four, times the wavelength of light, times your f-number.
Its width is 2.44 × the wavelength of light × your f-number.
D
Green light at f eight makes a disc about eleven microns wide. A Canon R8 pixel is six. So, about two pixels.
Green light at f/8 makes a disc about 11 microns wide. A Canon R8 pixel is 6. So, about 2 pixels.
E
Now f twenty-two. About thirty microns. Five pixels wide. Every point of detail smears across five.
Now f/22. About 30 microns. 5 pixels wide. Every point of detail smears across 5.
F
Same scene. Same lens. Only the aperture changed.
G
Stopping down buys you depth of field, but costs you sharpness.
H
So smaller is not automatically sharper.
I
A smaller aperture can mean a softer photo.
J

youtube.title: Why f/22 Is Softer Than f/8 (The Airy Disk, Simulated)
youtube.description:
Stopping down to f/22 spreads every point of light into an Airy disk about 2.44 × wavelength × f-number wide. For green light (~550 nm) that is ~11 µm at f/8 and ~30 µm at f/22. A Canon R8 pixel is 6 µm, so the disc covers ~2 pixels at f/8 and ~5 at f/22, which is why fine detail softens. The trade-off: stopping down buys depth of field. The star-chart comparison is a simulation of an ideal lens with diffraction only.
#photography #camera #shorts
